summary:
Jigawa State stands under Nigeria's national framework as well as its own state code. Nigeria criminalises same-sex conduct nationally under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), and the law reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and states that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

Jigawa is one of the twelve northern states carrying that additional Sharia layer. Human Rights Watch (2004) records Zamfara's governor as the first to extend Sharia to criminal law, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, and notes that by 2002 twelve northern states, Jigawa among them, had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation; these remain the only states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

Jigawa's own instrument is the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed on 18 December 2000 and brought into operation on 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12). The sourcebook places Jigawa among the four states, with Gombe, Kano and Zamfara, whose sodomy offence punishes unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm); lesbianism carries up to 50 lashes plus up to six months' imprisonment, and Jigawa's text includes an 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation of the offence. The state code criminalises conduct the federal code does not reach, women's same-sex conduct included.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country note lists Jigawa in a twelve-state Sharia penalties table under a Sharia Penal Code (2000): married men face death by stoning, unmarried men 100 lashes and imprisonment of up to one year, and same-sex acts between women up to 50 lashes with imprisonment of up to six months. Section 8.2.20 of the note covers the Sharia codes in force in Kano, Borno, Kaduna and other northern states, and the note confirms that the Sharia penal layer remains the operative criminal frame for Muslims in Jigawa.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.
tangentialFactors:
Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement nationwide. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

The principal trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
localsOnly:
Residents of Jigawa face two overlapping criminal layers. Muslims in the state are subject to the Sharia Penal Code Law 2000 as the operative criminal frame for their conduct, while the federal SSMPA applies to everyone regardless of faith. Jigawa is among the twelve states where Sharia courts hold jurisdiction to try criminal cases, so a prosecution for same-sex conduct can be heard in a Sharia court rather than a secular one.

The state code reaches further than the federal statute in both directions of sex. It fixes specific penalties for women's same-sex conduct, up to 50 lashes plus up to six months' imprisonment, an offence the federal code does not create, and it defines the sodomy offence through an 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation. Unmarried men face 100 lashes and up to one year's imprisonment; married men face stoning to death.

For Muslim men who are married, the stoning provision is written into the statute in force since 27 December 2000, and the UK Home Office's June 2025 note reproduces that penalty against Jigawa in its Sharia penalties table. Cohabitation, public display of a same-sex relationship and membership or operation of gay organisations remain separately punishable under the national act with 10 to 14 years' imprisonment.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing have been enacted into law remains unresolved on the sources available here; Reuters reported the proposals in September 2022 without confirmation of passage.

No Jigawa-specific enforcement record is sourced: these materials supply the text and penalties of the state code and its listing in a national country note, but no prosecution counts, sentencing outcomes or reported raids from Jigawa itself.

The application frequency of the stoning and lashing provisions is not sourced here. The figures above are the penalties as written and as reproduced in the UK Home Office table; how often Jigawa courts impose them is not established by this inventory.

No trans-specific violence, killing or custodial placement case from Jigawa appears in these sources; the documented trans cases (Abuja Area Mama, Bobrisky) occurred elsewhere in Nigeria.

Whether a foreign trans visitor would be processed under the Sharia penal layer or the federal statute in a given encounter, and whether immigration screening at entry engages gender markers, is not addressed by any source in this inventory.
